Buyer's Guide: What Actually Matters

Six things decide whether a socket set fits your jobs. Ignore the headline piece count; check these.

01

6-point vs 12-point

A socket's points are the corners of the star inside it. A 6-point socket grips the flat sides of a bolt head, spreading the force — it is stronger and far less likely to round a tight, rusty or damaged fastener. A 12-point socket meets the fastener at twice as many angles, so it slips on easily in tight spaces, but it bears on the corners and can round them under real torque. Rule of thumb: 6-point for force and old hardware, 12-point for speed and clean, low-torque assembly.

02

Drive sizes: 1/4 vs 3/8 vs 1/2

The drive is the square hole the ratchet plugs into, and it decides the size class. 1/4 in. is for small fasteners — trim, appliances, bikes — where feel beats force. 3/8 in. is the all-rounder that turns most car and home fasteners and the drive to own first. 1/2 in. is the heavy end: lug nuts, suspension and axle work, and the standard drive for impact wrenches. A complete garage eventually owns all three; a starter set should at least cover 3/8 in. well.

03

Shallow vs deep

Shallow sockets are the default — short, strong, and they fit where heads barely clear. Deep sockets exist for nuts threaded far down a stud, recessed bolts and spark plugs: anywhere the fastener sits at the bottom of a hole or the top of a long thread. Sets that include both depths of every size (the TEKTON and the NEIKO on this page) save you the second purchase the first time a shallow socket comes up short.

04

Chrome sockets vs impact sockets

Never put a shiny chrome hand socket on an impact wrench. Chrome sockets are hard and brittle; the hammering action of an impact gun can crack or shatter them, which is a safety problem, not just a broken tool. Impact sockets are built differently: thicker walls, tougher heat treatment, a black finish, and a little give engineered in so they absorb the blows. The NEIKO is the impact-rated set here; the other four are hand sockets for ratchets and breaker bars, where they belong.

05

No skipped sizes

A gap in the range is a trip to the store in the middle of a job. Good sets run a continuous ladder — every millimeter and every fraction in their span, in both depths. TEKTON builds its name on this (no skipped sizes across 4–38 mm), and the NEIKO does the same inside its 1/2 in. impact ranges. When you compare sets, read the size list, not the piece count: a 214-piece set with a hole at 18 mm is smaller than it looks.

06

Storage: rails, drawers or cases

How a set stores is how organized it stays. Rails and trays (TEKTON) suit a tool-chest drawer in a fixed workshop. A drawer box (GEARWRENCH) keeps a big kit sorted and portable. Blow-mold cases (EPAuto, Amazon Basics, NEIKO) travel anywhere, with a molded slot per piece — though retention varies, and the Amazon Basics case is known for letting sockets pop loose if it is carried carelessly. Pick the storage that matches where the work happens.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best socket set for most people?

It depends on the job you actually have. If sockets are the job, the TEKTON SHD99202 is the complete answer: 214 six-point sockets in every size across all three drive sizes, shallow and deep, with a lifetime warranty. If you are setting up a first household kit and need wrenches and hex keys in the same box, the Amazon Basics 201-piece is the safer first buy, and the GEARWRENCH 80942 is the step up for regular car work.

Should I buy 6-point or 12-point sockets?

For most home and car work, 6-point. A 6-point socket grips the flat sides of a bolt head, so it is far less likely to round off a tight, rusty or damaged fastener. A 12-point socket engages at twice as many angles, which makes it easier to slip onto a bolt in a tight space — useful for assembly work and low-torque fasteners. Pros often own 12-point for speed and 6-point for force. If you only buy one style, buy 6-point.

What drive size do I need — 1/4, 3/8 or 1/2 inch?

3/8 inch is the workhorse: it covers most car and home fasteners and is the drive to own first. 1/4 inch is for small fasteners — interior trim, appliances, electronics-adjacent work — where feel matters more than force. 1/2 inch is the heavy end: lug nuts, suspension bolts and anything that needs real torque, and it is the standard drive for impact wrenches. Sets like the TEKTON and the Amazon Basics cover all three; the EPAuto covers 1/4 and 3/8 only.

Can I use regular chrome sockets on an impact wrench?

No — this is the one safety rule on this page. Shiny chrome hand sockets are hard and brittle; the hammering of an impact wrench can crack or shatter them. Impact sockets are built for the job: thicker walls, tougher heat treatment and a black finish instead of chrome. If you run an impact wrench, use a rated impact set like the NEIKO 02448A, and keep your chrome sockets on hand ratchets where they belong.

Why do piece counts vary so much between sets?

Because brands count everything in the box. A 201-piece set is not 201 sockets — the count usually includes hex keys, driver bits, adapters and sometimes wrenches alongside the sockets. Compare the socket count and the size range, not the headline number. The TEKTON is the honest exception on this page: its 214 pieces really are 214 sockets.

Why do prices here say 'check price' while ratings are shown?

Because we only print numbers we verified. Every star rating on this page was read from the product's Amazon listing in November 2026. Prices change with sales and coupons faster than any page can track, so rather than show a figure that may already be wrong, every price reads 'check price' and links to the live listing.
